Data Types

Introduction

Every value in R has a type. Understanding data types is important because different types behave differently when we perform calculations, comparisons, or transformations.

The most common basic data types in R are:

  • Numeric
  • Integer
  • Character
  • Logical
  • Complex

R also has special values such as NA, NULL, NaN, and Inf.

Numeric

Numeric values represent numbers with decimal values.

x <- 10
y <- 3.14

x
[1] 10
y
[1] 3.14

Check the type:

typeof(x)
[1] "double"
typeof(y)
[1] "double"

Both are stored as:

double

In R, regular numeric values are generally stored as double-precision floating-point numbers.

Example

price <- 19.99
temperature <- 23.5
average <- 87.25

Integer

Integers represent whole numbers.

An integer can be explicitly created by adding L:

x <- 10L

x
[1] 10
typeof(x)
[1] "integer"

The result is:

integer

Compare:

x <- 10
y <- 10L

typeof(x)
[1] "double"
typeof(y)
[1] "integer"

Output:

double
integer

Remember: 10 is normally stored as a double, while 10L is stored as an integer.

Character

Character values represent text.

They can be created using either single or double quotation marks.

name <- "Sujan"
country <- 'Germany'

name
[1] "Sujan"
country
[1] "Germany"

Check the type:

typeof(name)
[1] "character"

Output:

character

Combining strings

Use paste():

first_name <- "Sujan"
last_name <- "Karna"

paste(first_name, last_name)
[1] "Sujan Karna"

Or use paste0():

paste0(first_name, "_", last_name)
[1] "Sujan_Karna"

The difference is that paste() inserts a separator by default, while paste0() does not.

paste("Hello", "World")
[1] "Hello World"
paste0("Hello", "World")
[1] "HelloWorld"

Logical

Logical values represent Boolean values.

R has two logical values:

TRUE
FALSE

Example:

is_student <- TRUE
has_license <- FALSE

is_student
[1] TRUE
has_license
[1] FALSE

Check the type:

typeof(is_student)
[1] "logical"

Output:

logical

Logical expressions

Comparisons produce logical values:

x <- 20

x > 10
[1] TRUE
x < 10
[1] FALSE
x == 20
[1] TRUE
x != 20
[1] FALSE

Output:

TRUE
FALSE
TRUE
FALSE

Complex

R supports complex numbers.

z <- 2 + 3i

z
[1] 2+3i
typeof(z)
[1] "complex"

The i represents the imaginary component.

You can access the real and imaginary parts:

Re(z)
[1] 2
Im(z)
[1] 3

Checking Data Types

R provides several functions for inspecting objects.

typeof()

typeof() tells you the underlying storage type.

x <- 10
typeof(x)
[1] "double"

class()

class() tells you the object’s class.

x <- 10
class(x)
[1] "numeric"

For many basic objects, typeof() and class() may give similar results, but they answer different questions.

Type-checking functions

R provides functions that return TRUE or FALSE.

is.numeric(10)
[1] TRUE
is.character("Hello")
[1] TRUE
is.logical(TRUE)
[1] TRUE
is.integer(10L)
[1] TRUE

Some other useful functions:

is.double(10)
[1] TRUE
is.complex(2 + 3i)
[1] TRUE

Type Conversion

R allows values to be converted from one type to another.

Convert to numeric

x <- "100"

as.numeric(x)
[1] 100

Check:

typeof(as.numeric(x))
[1] "double"

Convert to character

x <- 100

as.character(x)
[1] "100"

Convert to integer

x <- 10.5

as.integer(x)
[1] 10

Note that conversion to integer removes the decimal part rather than rounding the value.

as.integer(10.9)
[1] 10
as.integer(10.1)
[1] 10

Convert to logical

as.logical(1)
[1] TRUE
as.logical(0)
[1] FALSE

Type Coercion

R automatically converts values when different types are combined.

Consider:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)

typeof(x)
[1] "double"

The vector is numeric.

Now combine a number with a character:

x <- c(1, 2, "3")

x
[1] "1" "2" "3"
typeof(x)
[1] "character"

R converts the numbers to character values.

This is called type coercion.

A simplified coercion hierarchy is:

logical → numeric → character

For example:

x <- c(TRUE, 10)

x
[1]  1 10
typeof(x)
[1] "double"

The logical value is converted to numeric.

Special Values

R has several special values that are important when working with data.

NA

NA represents a missing value.

x <- c(10, 20, NA, 40)

x
[1] 10 20 NA 40

Check for missing values:

is.na(x)
[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

This returns:

FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE

NULL

NULL represents the absence of a value.

x <- NULL

x
NULL

Check:

is.null(x)
[1] TRUE

NULL is different from NA.

  • NA means a value is missing.
  • NULL means there is no value.

NaN

NaN means Not a Number.

It can occur when an undefined numerical operation is performed.

0 / 0
[1] NaN

Check:

is.nan(0 / 0)
[1] TRUE

Inf

Inf represents positive infinity.

1 / 0
[1] Inf

Negative infinity:

-1 / 0
[1] -Inf

Check:

is.infinite(1 / 0)
[1] TRUE

Comparing Special Values

A common mistake is trying to compare NA using ==.

For example:

x <- NA

x == NA
[1] NA

The result is:

NA

Instead, use:

is.na(x)
[1] TRUE

Similarly:

is.nan(NaN)
[1] TRUE
is.infinite(Inf)
[1] TRUE
is.null(NULL)
[1] TRUE

Summary of Basic Data Types

Type Example typeof()
Numeric 10.5 double
Integer 10L integer
Character "Hello" character
Logical TRUE logical
Complex 2 + 3i complex

Important Special Values

Value Meaning
NA Missing value
NULL No value
NaN Not a Number
Inf Positive infinity
-Inf Negative infinity

Useful Commands

Command Purpose
typeof() Get underlying data type
class() Get object’s class
is.numeric() Check if numeric
is.character() Check if character
is.logical() Check if logical
is.integer() Check if integer
is.double() Check if double
is.complex() Check if complex
is.na() Check for missing values
is.null() Check for NULL
is.nan() Check for NaN
is.infinite() Check for infinity
as.numeric() Convert to numeric
as.character() Convert to character
as.integer() Convert to integer
as.logical() Convert to logical

Quick Practice

Try to predict the result before running each command.

Exercise 1

x <- 25
typeof(x)
[1] "double"

Exercise 2

x <- 25L
typeof(x)
[1] "integer"

Exercise 3

x <- c(1, 2, "3")
typeof(x)
[1] "character"

Exercise 4

x <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
typeof(x)
[1] "logical"

Exercise 5

x <- c(10, NA, 30)

is.na(x)
[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

Key Takeaways

  • R has several basic data types, including numeric, integer, character, logical, and complex.
  • typeof() identifies the underlying storage type.
  • class() identifies an object’s class.
  • is.*() functions are useful for checking types and special values.
  • as.*() functions are used for type conversion.
  • R automatically performs type coercion when combining different types.
  • NA represents missing data and should be checked using is.na().
  • NULL, NA, NaN, and Inf have different meanings.
